['### `orjson` or Response Model

If what you are looking for is performance, you are probably better off using a [Response Model](../tutorial/response-model.md) than an `orjson` response.

With a response model, FastAPI will use Pydantic to serialize the data to JSON, without using intermediate steps, like converting it with `jsonable_encoder`, which would happen in any other case.

And under the hood, Pydantic uses the same underlying Rust mechanisms as `orjson` to serialize to JSON, so you will already get the best performance with a response model.', 'Your reading of the code is right. Numbers below are from your exact versions — FastAPI 0.140.7, Pydantic 2.13.4, Python 3.13.
1 and 2 — intentional, and yes you can rely on generics
Any return annotation FastAPI can build a TypeAdapter for produces a response field, generics included:
route annotation                  response_field  response_class  fast path
-> (none)                         none            default         False
-> dict[str, Any]                 yes             default         True
-> list[dict[str, Any]]           yes             default         True
-> list[Any]                      yes             default         True
-> Any                            yes             default         True
-> MyModel                        yes             default         True
-> dict[str, Any] + ORJSONResponse yes            ORJSON          False
-> (none) + ORJSONResponse        none            ORJSON          False

Even bare -> Any gets one. The only ways to end up on the jsonable_encoder branch are to omit the annotation or to return a Response object yourself.
3 — prefer the return type, and don't set both
This is the part worth knowing. From fastapi/routing.py in 0.140.7:
# Use the fast path (dump_json) when no custom response
# class was set and a response field with a TypeAdapter
# exists. Serializes directly to JSON bytes via Pydantic's
# Rust core, skipping the intermediate Python dict +
# json.dumps() step.
use_dump_json = response_field is not None and isinstance(
    response_class, DefaultPlaceholder
)
Passing response_class=ORJSONResponse means response_class is no longer a DefaultPlaceholder, so use_dump_json is False — you keep the response field but drop to field.serialize → Python objects → ORJSONResponse.render(). Setting both is the slowest of the three arrangements, not the fastest. (Both ORJSONResponse and UJSONResponse carry @deprecated in fastapi/responses.py, so the warning you hit is real, not advisory folklore.)
4 — a model is faster than dict[str, Any], and both beat the encoder path badly
Serialization only, 20,000 iterations, best of 3, 20-key flat dict with one nested value:
 4.9 us   -> MyModel                        serialize_json  (fast path)
 6.1 us   -> dict[str, Any]                 serialize_json  (fast path)
13.3 us   -> dict[str, Any]                 serialize + json.dumps
48.4 us   no annotation + ORJSONResponse    jsonable_encoder + orjson.dumps
53.8 us   no annotation                     jsonable_encoder + json.dumps
 0.8 us   orjson.dumps(payload)             raw, for reference

The model wins by roughly 25% because Any has no static schema — pydantic-core has to infer each value's type at runtime, while a declared model compiles a specialized serializer.
The bigger point is the ~8x gap to the encoder rows, and it explains the deprecation: the expensive part was never json.dumps vs orjson.dumps, it was jsonable_encoder walking the object graph in Python. That's also why ORJSONResponse only ever bought ~10% here — it optimized the cheap half of the work. Absolute numbers scale with payload size and shape; the ratios held across runs.
5 — agreed, worth documenting
"return type or response model" is accurate but reads as if it means Pydantic models specifically. Two additions would have saved you the source dive: that any return annotation qualifies, dict[str, Any] included, and that setting a custom response_class silently opts you out of the fast path. The second one is the surprising half — it's easy to assume the two optimizations stack. Happy to open a docs PR if a maintainer wants it.', '## Custom response class

You can create your own custom response class, inheriting from `Response` and using it.

For example, let's say that you want to use [`orjson`](https://github.com/ijl/orjson) with some settings.

Let's say you want it to return indented and formatted JSON, so you want to use the orjson option `orjson.OPT_INDENT_2`.

You could create a `CustomORJSONResponse`. The main thing you have to do is create a `Response.render(content)` method that returns the content as `bytes`:

```python
from typing import Any

import orjson
from fastapi import FastAPI, Response

app = FastAPI()


class CustomORJSONResponse(Response):
    media_type = "application/json"

    def render(self, content: Any) -> bytes:
        assert orjson is not None, "orjson must be installed"
        return orjson.dumps(content, option=orjson.OPT_INDENT_2)


@app.get("/", response_class=CustomORJSONResponse)
async def main():
    return {"message": "Hello World"}
```

Now instead of returning:

```json
{"message": "Hello World"}
```

...this response will return:

```json
{
  "message": "Hello World"
}
```

Of course, you will probably find much better ways to take advantage of this than formatting JSON. 😉', "## Return a `Response`

You can return a `Response` or any sub-class of it.

*Note*

`JSONResponse` itself is a sub-class of `Response`.

And when you return a `Response`, **FastAPI** will pass it directly.

It won't do any data conversion with Pydantic models, it won't convert the contents to any type, etc.

This gives you a lot of **flexibility**. You can return any data type, override any data declaration or validation, etc.

It also gives you a lot of **responsibility**. You have to make sure that the data you return is correct, in the correct format, that it can be serialized, etc.", '## How a Response Model Works

When you declare a [Response Model - Return Type](../tutorial/response-model.md) in a path operation, **FastAPI** will use it to serialize the data to JSON, using Pydantic.

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()


class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    description: str | None = None
    price: float
    tax: float | None = None
    tags: list[str] = []


@app.post("/items/")
async def create_item(item: Item) -> Item:
    return item


@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items() -> list[Item]:
    return [
        Item(name="Portal Gun", price=42.0),
        Item(name="Plumbus", price=32.0),
    ]
```

As that will happen on the Rust side, the performance will be much better than if it was done with regular Python and the `JSONResponse` class.

When using a `response_model` or return type, FastAPI won't use the `jsonable_encoder` to convert the data (which would be slower) nor the `JSONResponse` class.

Instead it takes the JSON bytes generated with Pydantic using the response model (or return type) and returns a `Response` with the right media type for JSON directly (`application/json`).']

['## Using the `jsonable_encoder` in a `Response`

Because **FastAPI** doesn't make any changes to a `Response` you return, you have to make sure its contents are ready for it.

For example, you cannot put a Pydantic model in a `JSONResponse` without first converting it to a `dict` with all the data types (like `datetime`, `UUID`, etc) converted to JSON-compatible types.

For those cases, you can use the `jsonable_encoder` to convert your data before passing it to a response:

```python
from datetime import datetime

from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.encoders import jsonable_encoder
from fastapi.responses import JSONResponse
from pydantic import BaseModel


class Item(BaseModel):
    title: str
    timestamp: datetime
    description: str | None = None


app = FastAPI()


@app.put("/items/{id}")
def update_item(id: str, item: Item):
    json_compatible_item_data = jsonable_encoder(item)
    return JSONResponse(content=json_compatible_item_data)
```

*Note: Technical Details*

You could also use `from starlette.responses import JSONResponse`.

**FastAPI** provides the same `starlette.responses` as `fastapi.responses` just as a convenience for you, the developer. But most of the available responses come directly from Starlette.', "## JSON Responses

By default FastAPI returns JSON responses.

If you declare a [Response Model](../tutorial/response-model.md) FastAPI will use it to serialize the data to JSON, using Pydantic.

If you don't declare a response model, FastAPI will use the `jsonable_encoder` explained in [JSON Compatible Encoder](../tutorial/encoder.md) and put it in a `JSONResponse`.

If you declare a `response_class` with a JSON media type (`application/json`), like is the case with the `JSONResponse`, the data you return will be automatically converted (and filtered) with any Pydantic `response_model` that you declared in the *path operation decorator*. But the data won't be serialized to JSON bytes with Pydantic, instead it will be converted with the `jsonable_encoder` and then passed to the `JSONResponse` class, which will serialize it to bytes using the standard JSON library in Python.", '## Exclude from OpenAPI

To exclude a *path operation* from the generated OpenAPI schema (and thus, from the automatic documentation systems), use the parameter `include_in_schema` and set it to `False`:

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI()


@app.get("/items/", include_in_schema=False)
async def read_items():
    return [{"item_id": "Foo"}]
```', '# JSON with Bytes as Base64

If your app needs to receive and send JSON data, but you need to include binary data in it, you can encode it as base64.', '### JSON Performance

In short, if you want the maximum performance, use a [Response Model](../tutorial/response-model.md) and don't declare a `response_class` in the *path operation decorator*.

```python
@app.post("/items/")
async def create_item(item: Item) -> Item:
    return item
```']

['### Async Context Manager

If you check, the function is decorated with an `@asynccontextmanager`.

That converts the function into something called an "**async context manager**".

```python
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

from fastapi import FastAPI


def fake_answer_to_everything_ml_model(x: float):
    return x * 42


ml_models = {}


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    # Load the ML model
    ml_models["answer_to_everything"] = fake_answer_to_everything_ml_model
    yield
    # Clean up the ML models and release the resources
    ml_models.clear()


app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)


@app.get("/predict")
async def predict(x: float):
    result = ml_models["answer_to_everything"](x)
    return {"result": result}
```

A **context manager** in Python is something that you can use in a `with` statement, for example, `open()` can be used as a context manager:

```Python
with open("file.txt") as file:
    file.read()
```

In recent versions of Python, there's also an **async context manager**. You would use it with `async with`:

```Python
async with lifespan(app):
    await do_stuff()
```

When you create a context manager or an async context manager like above, what it does is that, before entering the `with` block, it will execute the code before the `yield`, and after exiting the `with` block, it will execute the code after the `yield`.

In our code example above, we don't use it directly, but we pass it to FastAPI for it to use it.

The `lifespan` parameter of the `FastAPI` app takes an **async context manager**, so we can pass our new `lifespan` async context manager to it.

```python
from contextlib import asynccontextmanager

from fastapi import FastAPI


def fake_answer_to_everything_ml_model(x: float):
    return x * 42


ml_models = {}


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app: FastAPI):
    # Load the ML model
    ml_models["answer_to_everything"] = fake_answer_to_everything_ml_model
    yield
    # Clean up the ML models and release the resources
    ml_models.clear()


app = FastAPI(lifespan=lifespan)


@app.get("/predict")
async def predict(x: float):
    result = ml_models["answer_to_everything"](x)
    return {"result": result}
```', '## Allowing Requests Without Content-Type

If you need to support clients that don't send a `Content-Type` header, you can disable strict checking by setting `strict_content_type=False`:

from fastapi import FastAPI

app = FastAPI(strict_content_type=False)


class Item(BaseModel):
    name: str
    price: float


@app.post("/items/")
async def create_item(item: Item):
    return item
```

With this setting, requests without a `Content-Type` header will have their body parsed as JSON, which is the same behavior as older versions of FastAPI.

*Note*

This behavior and configuration was added in FastAPI 0.132.0.', '## `HTTPSRedirectMiddleware`

Enforces that all incoming requests must either be `https` or `wss`.

Any incoming request to `http` or `ws` will be redirected to the secure scheme instead.

```python
from fastapi import FastAPI
from fastapi.middleware.httpsredirect import HTTPSRedirectMiddleware

app = FastAPI()

app.add_middleware(HTTPSRedirectMiddleware)


@app.get("/")
async def main():
    return {"message": "Hello World"}
```', '# Strict Content-Type Checking

By default, **FastAPI** uses strict `Content-Type` header checking for JSON request bodies, this means that JSON requests **must** include a valid `Content-Type` header (e.g. `application/json`) in order for the body to be parsed as JSON.', '## Parameterize the instance

And now, we can use `__init__` to declare the parameters of the instance that we can use to "parameterize" the dependency:

```python
from typing import Annotated

Thanks for confirming this Sergei @yudin-s, and for the fix. Moving __enter__ out of the try fixes the first issue cleanly (and it also stops __exit__ swallowing the __enter__ exception when it returned True, which the old except block used to do).
I kept digging and found two more deviations from PEP 343 that the fix alone does not cover.
2. except Exception skips BaseException
The guard catches Exception but not BaseException. So KeyboardInterrupt, SystemExit, and asyncio.CancelledError raised in the body never reach __exit__. A standard with calls __exit__ for all of these:
class T:
    def __enter__(self): return self
    def __exit__(self, *a):
        print("exit called", a[0])
        return False

try:
    with T():
        raise KeyboardInterrupt()
except KeyboardInterrupt:
    pass
# standard with: exit runs, receives KeyboardInterrupt
# contextmanager_in_threadpool: exit never runs
So the guard needs to be except BaseException.
3. Real anyio cancellation never reaches __exit__
This one is sneakier. Even with except BaseException, a real task cancellation (via cancel_scope.cancel()) still does not run __exit__. The await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(...) call is itself a checkpoint: anyio sees the scope is still cancelled and re-raises CancelledError before the worker thread starts.
I confirmed this by canceling a task group child parked inside the context:
async with anyio.create_task_group() as tg:
    async def child():
        async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm):
            await anyio.sleep(10)
    tg.start_soon(child)
    await anyio.sleep(0.1)
    tg.cancel_scope.cancel()
# cm.exit_called == False
That is the worst case for cleanup: cancellation is exactly when you want __exit__ to run, and it is exactly when it gets skipped.
4. The else (normal exit) branch has the same hole
The else branch runs __exit__(None, None, None) after a body that completed without raising. Its await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(...) is a checkpoint too. If a cancel lands in the window between a checkpoint-free body returning and that await, __exit__ is skipped while __enter__ already ran - a straight resource leak. Reproducible:
async with anyio.create_task_group() as tg:
    async def child():
        async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm):
            entered.set()   # body has no other await
    tg.start_soon(child)
    await entered.wait()
    tg.cancel_scope.cancel()
# without a shield on the else branch: cm.exit_called == False
# enter ran, exit did not
That window is narrow, but it is real. For a cleanup callback it should not exist at all.
Fix: shield every __exit__ thread call
exit_limiter = CapacityLimiter(1)
value = await run_in_threadpool(cm.__enter__)
try:
    yield value
except BaseException as e:
    with anyio.CancelScope(shield=True):
        ok = bool(
            await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(
                cm.__exit__, type(e), e, e.__traceback__, limiter=exit_limiter
            )
        )
    if not ok:
        raise
else:
    with anyio.CancelScope(shield=True):
        await anyio.to_thread.run_sync(
            cm.__exit__, None, None, None, limiter=exit_limiter
        )
Both __exit__ calls are now shielded. The mental model is simple: once __enter__ has run, __exit__ always runs to completion, cancellation or not. This mirrors what a synchronous with already does: __exit__ is a sync call, you cannot cancel it mid-flight.
Here are the tests that pin each of the cases above, so it is not just a claim. All run on both asyncio and trio (@pytest.mark.anyio), so the asyncio and trio variants are separate test items.
class EnterFailsCM:
    def __init__(self, exit_return: bool | None = False) -> None:
        self.exit_called = False
        self.exit_return = exit_return

    def __enter__(self) -> str:
        raise ValueError("setup failed")

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb) -> bool | None:
        self.exit_called = True
        return self.exit_return


@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_enter_failure_does_not_call_exit() -> None:
    cm = EnterFailsCM()
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="setup failed"):
        async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm):
            pass
    assert not cm.exit_called


@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_enter_failure_propagates_even_if_exit_would_suppress() -> None:
    # old code: __exit__(True) would swallow the __enter__ ValueError
    cm = EnterFailsCM(exit_return=True)
    with pytest.raises(ValueError, match="setup failed"):
        async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm):
            pass
    assert not cm.exit_called


class ExitTrackingCM:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.exit_called = False
        self.exit_args: tuple = ()

    def __enter__(self) -> str:
        return "value"

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb) -> bool:
        self.exit_called = True
        self.exit_args = (exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb)
        return False


@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_keyboard_interrupt_in_body_calls_exit() -> None:
    cm = ExitTrackingCM()
    with pytest.raises(KeyboardInterrupt, match="boom"):
        async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm):
            raise KeyboardInterrupt("boom")
    assert cm.exit_called
    assert cm.exit_args[0] is KeyboardInterrupt


# SystemExit and manual asyncio.CancelledError are covered by two more tests
# of the same shape (test_system_exit_in_body_calls_exit,
# test_cancelled_error_in_body_calls_exit).


class SlowExitTrackingCM:
    def __init__(self) -> None:
        self.exit_called = False

    def __enter__(self) -> str:
        return "value"

    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb) -> bool:
        self.exit_called = True
        return False


@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_real_cancellation_still_calls_exit() -> None:
    import anyio

    cm = SlowExitTrackingCM()

    async with anyio.create_task_group() as tg:
        async def child() -> None:
            async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm):
                await anyio.sleep(10)

        tg.start_soon(child)
        await anyio.sleep(0.1)
        tg.cancel_scope.cancel()

    assert cm.exit_called


@pytest.mark.anyio
async def test_cancellation_after_normal_body_still_calls_exit() -> None:
    import anyio

    cm = SlowExitTrackingCM()
    entered = anyio.Event()

    async with anyio.create_task_group() as tg:
        async def child() -> None:
            async with contextmanager_in_threadpool(cm):
                entered.set()

        tg.start_soon(child)
        await entered.wait()
        tg.cancel_scope.cancel()

    assert cm.exit_called
The last test is the one that made me add the shield on the else branch too: without it, assert cm.exit_called fails on the asyncio backend (enter ran, exit did not). With the shield, it passes on both backends.
I have a full set of tests covering these cases locally. An earlier version went up as a PR but got closed/rejected, so I reworked it: the enter-out-of-try, the BaseException guard, and the shields on both branches are all pinned by tests now, on both asyncio and trio.
One tradeoff to flag: if __exit__ blocks (rollback to a dead DB), cancellation cannot interrupt it until __exit__ returns. That is the same constraint as a plain with, but it is worth being explicit about it.
